newsitem.title: GERMANY: Issing-don't give "outs" access to ECB Euro credit.
newsitem.headline: Issing-don't give "outs" access to ECB Euro credit.

text.p: Bundesbank directorate member Otmar Issing on Thursday reiterated the Bundesbank's opposition to giving European Union members outside monetary union access to intraday or overnight credit in Euros as part of the "Target" settlement system.

Referring to recent demands that the central banks of countries outside the planned monetary union should have the same access to the Target system as the banks of monetary union members, Issing said this would be unprecedented.
"No central bank has, to date, let another take part in its own money creation."
Issing made the comments in the text of a speech due to be delivered at a conference in Luxembourg. The Bundesbank made the text available in Frankfurt.

Issing said giving non-members, or "outs", equal access to Target as EMU members would result in central banks outside the Euro currency area gaining access to intraday or overnight refinancing credits in Euros at the future European Central Bank.
Issing said preventing "outs" from gaining equal access would not be discriminatory. "The principle of non- discrimination means treating equal things equally and unequal things unequally.

"If a country does not take part in the third stage (of monetary union) and thereby remains outside the Euro currency area, it cannot make a legitimate claim to a refinancing at a central bank which issues a different currency, even if it is only during the day."
Giving "out" central banks access to such Euro credits would amount to unjustifiable favouritism against the members of monetary union, Issing said.
The central banks of EMU member countries will differ from others in that they will pursue a uniform monetary policy and possibly apply minimum reserve requirements, Issing said.

"Based on these differences "out" central banks may be in a position to treat their commercial banks more favourably than the "in" central banks if they gain unhindered access to Euro refinancing loans," Issing said.
The power to create central bank money in Euros must be the exclusive domain of the European system of central banks, he said.
Money creation by an "out" central bank would disrupt the monetary policy of the European central bank, even if the size and duration were limited, Issing said.
"Granting an intraday credit to the central bank of a non-participant can boost liquidity in a way that is relevant to monetary policy," Issing said.
"Intraday credit can splash over into overnight credit and thereby change central bank money supply and affect control of the money market.
"The call money rate would probably become more volatile and the need for fine-tuning measures would increase. The risk of wrong interest rate signals would increase."
In addition, the European central bank's monetary policy sovereignty could be undermined if "out" central bank resorted to unlimited intraday credit to support their own currencies.
"The ECB could thereby involuntarily contribute to the financing of speculation. The probability of a splashing over into overnight credit would increase considerably."
But Issing added that all central banks would be free to participate in the Target system provided that this not involve taking credit in Euros.
